A national zombie foreclosure rate of 3 percent sounds small. ATTOM's Q4 2026 report found 8,040 abandoned properties among the 269,195 in the foreclosure process.

Now look local. Zombie properties rose from the prior quarter in 29 states, including Pennsylvania (up 17.2 percent to 252) and Maryland (up 19.2 percent to 180). Baltimore had the highest metro zombie rate, at 13 percent.

Lenders can check vacancy and abandonment for the county or metro where the collateral sits, not just the national figure. A 3 percent average can hide a 13 percent market.

posts.text:
A rehab loan funds work on a house that already exists. A ground-up loan funds a house that does not exist yet, so the lender is financing something that is not built yet.

Draws are tied to building milestones and lender inspections, and the clock is longer: 3 to 9 months for a flip versus 12 to 24 for a build, per one lender guide.

Overruns scale. A 10 percent overrun is $8,500 on an $85,000 rehab and $32,000 on a $320,000 build (illustrative).

Overruns often fall on the borrower unless a contingency is built in, per one guide.

vaultedonline.com

posts.text:
Twenty loans can look diversified and still be one bet.

Picture 20 loans of $300,000 each, an illustrative book. If 8 sit in one flood-prone county, that is $2,400,000 of $6,000,000, or 40 percent of the book, exposed to a single storm.

Regulated lenders may not close a loan on property in a FEMA special flood hazard area without flood coverage. Other lenders may set their own rules. Most homeowners policies do not cover flood, and NFIP policies typically have a 30 day wait.

Lenders can map every loan by flood zone and confirm coverage before closing.

posts.text:
A wholesaler has a contract to buy a house for $140,000 and an end buyer lined up at $175,000. The first purchase needs cash before the resale pays anything.

A transactional loan can bridge that gap. Illustrative flow:

1. The lender funds the $140,000 purchase.
2. The investor resells to the end buyer for $175,000.
3. Sale proceeds repay the lender, $140,000 plus its fees.
4. The remaining $35,000, before fees and closing costs, is the investor's.

Repayment can come the same day, and one source says within a week at most. The resale is the repayment source.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Four step cards: lender funds a $140,000 purchase, investor resells for $175,000, lender is repaid $140,000 plus fees from the proceeds, investor keeps about $35,000 before fees. A bar splits the $175,000 resale into $140,000 and $35,000.

posts.text:
You received $12,000 in interest on private loans this year. Which IRS forms may be involved?

Three to know. Form 1099-INT: reports interest a business pays you, at $600 or more. Form 1098: filed by someone in a trade or business who receives $600 or more of mortgage interest from an individual. Schedule B: required with over $1,500 of taxable interest or ordinary dividends, among other cases.

The IRS says you must report all interest even without a 1099-INT.

Which forms apply varies. Ask your accountant. This is education, not tax advice.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Graphic titled Interest received? Three IRS forms to know. Illustrative $12,000 of interest. Cards: Form 1099-INT at $600 or more from a business, Form 1098 at $600 or more of mortgage interest, Schedule B over $1,500. Report interest either way; ask your accountant.

The New York Fed released its Q3 2026 household debt report on November 10. The flow of mortgage balances into serious delinquency, 90 or more days late, rose from 1.28% a year ago to 1.60%.

That is 0.32 points, or 25% more. The measure is balances newly 90 days late, divided by balances that were current or under 90 days late the quarter before.

If a $20,000,000 book moved the same way, 1.28% is $256,000 a year and 1.60% is $320,000. This covers consumer mortgage debt, not private loans, so use it as a backdrop and watch your own aging.

A lender wants to sell a performing loan. What might a buyer want to see in the file?

Loan purchase checklists point to a short list. The original promissory note, not a copy. Any allonge, the instrument that endorses the note to the next holder. The mortgage, with details that match the title policy. Recorded assignments. Payment history. Insurance, and whether coverage is adequate.

A buyer also needs to know if the borrower is in default before taking over.

This list is not exhaustive. Ask counsel what your deal needs.

posts.text:
What does federal law say about an IRA lending to the owner's daughter?

Federal law lists "lending of money or other extension of credit between a plan and a disqualified person" as a prohibited transaction. The Department of Labor says the term plan includes an IRA. The IRS says disqualified persons include the IRA owner's fiduciary and family: spouse, ancestor, lineal descendant, and any spouse of a lineal descendant.

The IRS also says a disqualified person who takes part in a prohibited transaction must pay a tax.

General education, not advice. Consult a qualified tax or legal professional first.

A $340,000 loan comes due in 12 months. The borrower plans to refinance. What if that fails?

The CFPB defines a balloon payment as "a large, one-time payment at the end of the loan term," and says that if property value or finances decline, the borrower might not be able to refinance.

Illustrative: a new lender refinances up to 75 percent of value. At $480,000, that is $360,000, enough to repay $340,000. If value falls to $420,000, it is $315,000. The gap is $25,000.

Lenders can re-check value and the exit plan well before maturity.

A borrower looks great on paper. What can a lender check before closing?

Identity: government ID can be checked against public records, and the person signing the note can be confirmed.

Litigation: court records can show lawsuits, judgments, bankruptcies and prior foreclosures.

Liens: a lien review can look for IRS tax liens, mechanics' liens or HOA super-liens.

Experience: a project history list can show addresses, purchase prices, sale prices and timelines.

An undisclosed prior foreclosure is far more useful to know before funding than after. What a lender checks varies by lender and by state.

A borrower asks to refinance a $400,000 property. Same risk as a rate-term refi? Not once cash leaves the deal.

Illustrative: the payoff is $210,000. A rate-term refinance replaces it, so the new loan is roughly $210,000 before costs, or 52.5% of value. Add $90,000 cash out and the loan is $300,000, or 75%. Equity falls from $190,000 to $100,000.

Fannie Mae caps cash back on its limited cash-out refinance at the greater of 1% of the new loan or $2,000.

Lenders can size leverage on the new loan, not the old payoff. Terms vary by lender.

posts.text:
A borrower gets a default notice on a loan with a $260,000 balance. How much does it take to stop the foreclosure?

It depends on the route.

Reinstatement brings the loan current in one lump sum: missed payments plus late fees and foreclosure costs, such as attorney fees. Suppose the quote is $9,000.

Payoff pays the whole remaining balance plus similar fees and costs. Here, that is $260,000 or more.

Whether a borrower has a right to reinstate varies by state and by the loan documents. Lenders can put each figure in a written quote.

General education, not legal advice.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Two comparison cards for an illustrative loan with a $260,000 balance and a default notice. Reinstatement: one lump sum to bring the loan current, illustrative quote $9,000. Payoff: the whole remaining balance plus fees and costs, $260,000 or more. Rights vary by state and loan documents.

sources.title: What's the Difference Between Reinstatement and Payoff in Foreclosure?
sources.quote: A 'reinstatement' occurs when the borrower brings the delinquent loan current in one lump sum. A 'payoff' occurs when the borrower pays the total amount required to satisfy the loan balance. The quote will include the unpaid principal balance and interest, plus any fees and costs.

sources.title: Reinstatement and Payoff to Prevent Foreclosure
sources.quote: Reinstatement involves making a single payment to catch up with everything due on a loan. State law may provide a deadline for reinstatement, or your mortgage or deed of trust may provide a deadline.

posts.text:
A title policy may not cover a boundary problem.

One reason is the survey exception. Standard title policies exclude matters that a correct survey would reveal, such as an encroachment, where a structure crosses a property line without legal authorization.

Once a survey flags one, the title company lists it as a specific exception. And if a building a lender funds sits partly on a neighbor's land, the lender's security interest is compromised.

Lenders can read the exceptions on a title commitment and ask whether a survey is needed. Requirements vary by state and by lender. Not legal advice.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Three step cards: the title policy excludes matters a correct survey would reveal; a survey flags an encroachment and the title company lists it as a specific exception; the lender weighs a building sitting partly on a neighbor's land. A panel says lenders can ask whether a survey is needed.

sources.title: Best Practices: The Survey Exception
sources.quote: Any encroachment, encumbrance, violation, variation, or adverse circumstance affecting the title

sources.title: What Happens If an ALTA Survey Reveals an Encroachment?
sources.quote: An encroachment happens when a structure or improvement crosses a property line without legal authorization. Standard title insurance policies exclude matters that a correct survey would reveal. Once an ALTA survey flags an encroachment, the title company lists it as a specific exception. If a building they fund sits partially on a neighbor’s land, their security interest is compromised.

sources.title: Title Policy May not Cover Boundary Disputes
sources.quote: The title insurance policy typically purchased by Buyers during escrow generally does not cover boundary defects.

posts.text:
A bank statement shows a balance. It does not show where the money came from.

For conventional purchase loans, Fannie Mae defines a large deposit as a single deposit over 50 percent of monthly qualifying income. If those funds are needed to close, the lender must document an acceptable source. Freddie Mac defines it differently.

Illustrative: on $7,000 a month, the line is $3,500. A $45,000 deposit is well over it.

Private lender policies may differ. Lenders may ask for documents showing the source before counting the cash.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Bar chart with an illustrative $45,000 single deposit far above a $3,500 line, which is 50 percent of $7,000 monthly income. Cards give the Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac large deposit tests and note that private lender policy varies.

sources.title: B3-4.2-02, Depository Accounts
sources.quote: A large deposit is defined as a single deposit that exceeds 50% of the total monthly qualifying income for the loan.

sources.title: B3-4.2-02, Depository Accounts
sources.quote: If funds from a large deposit are needed to complete the purchase transaction, the lender must document that those funds are from an acceptable source.

posts.text:
A title commitment arrives before closing. Where should a lender look?

Schedule A holds the basic facts: effective date, who is insured, amount of insurance, current owner and legal description.

Schedule B, Part I lists requirements to meet before the policy is issued, such as payments or documents that must be completed.

Schedule B, Part II lists exceptions, matters the policy will not cover. In the ALTA form, an exception can cover anything first appearing in the public records after the commitment date.

Lenders can check the insured and amount, then read every exception.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Three cards explain a title commitment. Schedule A lists the basic facts: effective date, who is insured, amount of insurance, current owner and legal description. Schedule B Part I lists requirements to meet before the policy is issued. Schedule B Part II lists exceptions, matters the policy will not cover.

sources.title: Understanding Your Title Commitment
sources.quote: The first part of Schedule B lists all the requirements that must be met before your policy will be issued. The second part of Schedule B lists the matters that will be exceptions in your policy, which are things not covered.

sources.title: ALTA Commitment for Title Insurance (7-1-21)
sources.publisher: American Land Title Association (form hosted by Stewart)
sources.quote: Any defect, lien, encumbrance, adverse claim, or other matter that appears for the first time in the Public Records or is created, attaches, or is disclosed between the Commitment Date and the date on which all of the Schedule B, Part I—Requirements are met.

posts.text:
A $4,800 tax bill and a $1,800 insurance premium. Who is watching them on your loan?

With escrow, the borrower usually sends one twelfth of each bill with every payment. $4,800 plus $1,800 is $6,600 a year, so $550 a month: $400 for tax and $150 for insurance. The servicer pays the bills.

Without escrow, the borrower pays both bills directly. Unpaid property taxes can become a lien on the property, and if a policy lapses a lender may buy its own coverage. Lenders may want proof that both are paid.

Terms vary by lender and by state.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Two rows of twelve monthly boxes. With escrow, each month shows $550, one twelfth of $4,800 tax plus $1,800 insurance. Without escrow, the borrower pays $4,800 and $1,800 directly in two lumps. Formula: ($4,800 + $1,800) divided by 12 equals $550. Amounts illustrative.
